content_metadata.description: The video demonstrates an experiment on studying electromagnetic properties of an appliance and calculating the internal current using the Biot-Savart Law. It includes detailed instructions on data collection and analysis.

qAndA.question: What tool is needed to measure the distance between the phone and the appliance?

qAndA.answer: Appliances that generate heat, such as toasters, microwaves, hair dryers, or in this case, an electric kettle.
qAndA.question: What types of appliances are recommended for this experiment?

qAndA.answer: The phone case has a magnet, which would interfere with the magnetometer readings.

What mode in the Phyphox app should be used for collecting the magnetic field data?
What is the approximate current flowing through the electric kettle based on the experiment's measurements?

narrativeProgression.description: The video explains that steady currents generate steady magnetic fields.
The video explains the magnetic field of a steady current carrying wire using the Biot-Savart Law.

narrativeProgression.description: The video explains that in North America, the wall current runs on alternating current, which will create a magnetic field around appliances.
The video explains that although the magnetic field will change at 60 Hz, the experiment will not measure the 60 Hz oscillation but rather the amplitude of the magnetic field.
The video states the objective of the experiment: to detect the changes in a magnetic field when a household appliance is turned on and off.
The video outlines the approach to the experiment.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: This experiment will study the electromagnetic properties of an appliance and measure the
internal current inside it using the magnetometer of your phone.
The idea here is that steady currents will generate steady magnetic fields following the
B.O. subart law.
The magnetic field of a steady current carrying wire is just given as B is equal to mu
not i over 2 pi r, where mu not is the permeability of free space, i is the current in the wire,
and r is the distance from the wire to wherever the magnetic field is being measured.
The figure here illustrates the application of the right hand rule to show where the magnetic
field is oriented.
In North America, the wall current runs on alternating current where the voltage oscillates
up and down with a frequency of 60 hertz.
This shows a typical graph of the voltage in an electrical line.
The period of the wave here is 160th of a second.
This shows the voltage on the vertical axis and time in the horizontal axis.
This changing current will actually create a magnetic field around appliances that are
drawing that current and that magnetic field will be changing also with 60 hertz.
And to note in this measurement, we will not be able to measure a 60 hertz oscillation
because of limitations in your phone sensors, but we will be seeing the change, specifically
we'll be seeing the amplitude of the magnetic field changing.
The objective of this lab is to detect the changes in a magnetic field when a household
appliance is turned both on and off.
We'll take the basic approach that we'll use the Firefox app on the phone to measure
the magnetic field when the appliance is turned on.
We'll estimate the distance between the magnetometer of the phone and the appliance, and we'll
use that to calculate the approximate current in the appliance using the B of Svart law.
For this lab, you will need to take a screenshot of the changing magnetic field and upload it
to E-class and then answer a few short questions in an E-class lab questionnaire where you'll
show your calculations and describe a bit about your setup.
Let's take a look at how to collect data.
To collect data in this lab, you will need a ruler or something to measure distance with.
Your smartphone running the Firefox app and an electrical appliance.
The kind of appliances that work best are things that do heating.
For example, this is an electric kettle, a toaster oven works well, microwaves work well,
as do hair dryers.
You'll want something that draws a lot of current so we get a strong signal.
The way we'll collect data is we'll take the Firefox app.
We'll remove it from my phone, from the case because my case has a magnet in it and I'll
collect some data.
What I'll need to do is turn things around so that I zero out the magnetometer.
Then I'll want to pause collecting data and place the phone next to the appliance.

What I want to do is let it collect some data, turn on the appliance, notice the change
in the magnetic field and then turn off the appliance.

Then we'll want to measure the distance from the center of the appliance to where your
phone's magnetometer is.

That's about 42.4 to 43.6.
